quotes.t: Life does not cease to be funny when people die any more than it ceases to be serious when people laugh.
He who has never hoped can never despair.
Self-sacrifice enables us to sacrifice other people without blushing.
quotes.source: Man and Superman (1903), "Maxims for Revolutionists: Self-Sacrifice"

quotes.t: I have nothing but contempt for the kind of Governor who is afraid, for whatever reason, to follow the course that he knows is best for the State.
When a man has lost all happiness, he's not alive. Call him a breathing corpse.
Heaven ne'er helps the men who will not act.
A man is truly ethical only when he obeys the compulsion to help all life which he is able to assist, and shrinks from injuring anything that lives.
Life becomes harder for us when we live for others, but it also becomes richer and happier.

I can do no other than be reverent before everything that is called life. I can do no other than to have compassion for all that is called life. That is the beginning and the foundation of all ethics.
Four hostile newspapers are more to be feared than a thousand bayonets.
A throne is only a bench covered with velvet.
Among those who dislike oppression are many who like to oppress.
To live is to be willing to die over and over again.
The essence of bravery is being without self-deception.
The root of suffering is resisting the certainty that no matter what the circumstances, uncertainty is all we truly have.
To forget one's ancestors is to be a brook without a source, a tree without a root.
Better a diamond with a flaw than a pebble without one.
A man who cannot tolerate small misfortunes can never accomplish great things.
How many things I can do without!
quotes.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers, II.25

quotes.t: A man who is good for anything ought not to calculate the chance of living or dying; he ought only to consider whether in doing anything he is doing right or wrong — acting the part of a good man or a bad.
Wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder.
As if you could kill time without injuring eternity.
You must live in the present, launch yourself on every wave, find your eternity in each moment.
Only that day dawns to which we are awake.
When dharma does not fill your whole body and mind, you think it is already sufficient. When dharma fills your body and mind, you understand that something is missing.
When you paint Spring, do not paint willows, plums, peaches, or apricots, but just paint Spring.
Do not arouse disdainful mind when you prepare a broth of wild grasses; do not arouse joyful mind when you prepare a fine cream soup.
The ambition of the greatest man of our generation has been to wipe every tear from every eye.
At the dawn of history India started on her unending quest, and trackless centuries are filled with her striving and the grandeur of her successes and her failures.
We end today a period of ill fortune and India discovers herself again.
There is in every one of us, even those who seem to be most moderate, a type of desire that is terrible, wild, and lawless.
The object of education is to teach us to love what is beautiful.
No law or ordinance is mightier than knowledge.
The secret of being a bore is to tell everything.
quotes.source: Sept Discours en Vers sur l'Homme (1738), Sixth Discourse

quotes.t: Our wretched species is so made that those who walk on the well-trodden path always throw stones at those who are showing a new road.
The superfluous, a very necessary thing.
There is no frigate like a book to take us lands away, nor any coursers like a page of prancing poetry.
The heart asks pleasure first, and then, excuse from pain.
Pain has an element of blank.
Charity begins at home, and justice begins next door.
The sun himself is weak when he first rises, and gathers strength and courage as the day gets on.
Though home is a name, a word, it is a strong one; stronger than magician ever spoke, or spirit answered to, in strongest conjuration.
A slip of the foot you may soon recover, but a slip of the tongue you may never get over.
Energy and persistence conquer all things.
Anger is never without a reason, but seldom with a good one.
We must constantly build dykes of courage to hold back the flood of fear.
Shallow understanding from people of good will is more frustrating than absolute misunderstanding from people of ill will.
There can be no deep disappointment where there is not deep love.
A large income is the best recipe for happiness I ever heard of.
Every man is surrounded by a neighbourhood of voluntary spies.
We have all a better guide in ourselves, if we would attend to it, than any other person can be.
Music is the shorthand of emotion.
The sole meaning of life is to serve humanity by contributing to the establishment of the kingdom of God, which can only be done by the recognition and profession of the truth by every man.
quotes.source: The Kingdom of God Is Within You, ch. XII (1894)

quotes.t: Man cannot possess anything as long as he fears death. But to him who does not fear it, everything belongs.
quotes.source: War and Peace, Book XV, ch. 1

quotes.t: But how could you live and have no story to tell?
Every man has reminiscences which he would not tell to everyone, but only to his friends.
quotes.source: Notes from Underground (1864), Part I, ch. 2

quotes.t: It seems, in fact, as though the second half of a man's life is made up of nothing but the habits he has accumulated during the first half.
Nothing in this world is harder than speaking the truth, nothing easier than flattery.
Man is unhappy because he doesn't know he's happy. It's only that.
Love is such a priceless treasure that you can redeem the whole world by it, and expiate not only your own sins but the sins of others.
quotes.source: The Brothers Karamazov, Book II, ch. 3 (1880)

quotes.t: The weak fall, but the strong will remain and never go under!
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl (entry of 11 April 1944)

quotes.t: You don't choose your family. They are God's gift to you, as you are to them.
quotes.source: Address at his enthronement as Anglican Archbishop of Cape Town, 7 September 1986

quotes.t: If you do not breathe through writing, if you do not cry out in writing, or sing in writing, then don't write, because our culture has no use for it.
quotes.source: "The New Woman", in In Favor of the Sensitive Man and Other Essays (1976)

quotes.t: Many receive advice, few profit by it.
Our grand business undoubtedly is, not to see what lies dimly at a distance, but to do what lies clearly at hand.
No need to hurry. No need to sparkle. No need to be anybody but oneself.
quotes.source: A Room of One's Own, Chapter 1 (1929)

quotes.t: Nothing contributes so much to tranquillize the mind as a steady purpose,—a point on which the soul may fix its intellectual eye.
quotes.source: Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus, Letter 1 (1818)

quotes.t: A Poet is the most unpoetical of anything in existence; because he has no Identity—he is continually in for—and filling some other Body.
Simple can be harder than complex: You have to work hard to get your thinking clean to make it simple. But it's worth it in the end because once you get there, you can move mountains.
An ideal society should be mobile, should be full of channels for conveying a change taking place in one part to other parts.
The observer is the observed.
quotes.source: The Collected Works of J. Krishnamurti (1945–1948)

quotes.t: Your friend is the man who knows all about you, and still likes you.
quotes.source: The Note Book of Elbert Hubbard (1927)

quotes.t: The glow of one warm thought is to me worth more than money.
Let others praise ancient times; I am glad I was born in these.
If only one could tell true love from false love as one can tell mushrooms from toadstools.
Prejudices, it is well known, are most difficult to eradicate from the heart whose soil has never been loosened or fertilised by education: they grow there, firm as weeds among stones.
A morning-glory at my window satisfies me more than the metaphysics of books.
quotes.source: "Song of Myself", section 24, Leaves of Grass (1855)

quotes.t: The greater the difficulty, the greater the glory.
quotes.source: De Officiis, Book I, section 64 (44 BC)

quotes.t: The test of a civilization is in the way that it cares for its helpless members.
Worry pretends to be necessary but serves no useful purpose.
From that moment, I understood the pathway from slavery to freedom.
quotes.source: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (1845)

quotes.t: You confuse two things: solving a problem and stating a problem correctly. It is only the second that is obligatory for an artist.
Hope is the sun. It is light. It is passion. It is the fundamental force for life's blossoming.
The man who has no imagination has no wings.
What you get by achieving your goals is not as important as what you become by achieving your goals.
The most important thing is to try and inspire people so that they can be great in whatever they want to do.
The sea, the great unifier, is man's only hope. Now, as never before, the old phrase has a literal meaning: we are all in the same boat.
No matter what anybody tells you, words and ideas can change the world.
If we can teach people about wildlife, they will be touched. Share my wildlife with me. Because humans want to save things that they love.
I always knew I was a star. And now, the rest of the world seems to agree with me.
It's easier to ask forgiveness than it is to get permission.
When I was young, my ambition was to be one of the people who made a difference in this world. My hope is to leave the world a little better for having been there.
No water, no life. No blue, no green.
quotes.source: "My wish: Protect our oceans", TED Talk (2009)

quotes.t: Working hard for something we don't care about is called stress; working hard for something we love is called passion.
The truth is, most of us discover where we are headed when we arrive.
There may be times when we are powerless to prevent injustice, but there must never be a time when we fail to protest.
quotes.source: Nobel Lecture, "Hope, Despair and Memory", 11 December 1986

quotes.t: First forget inspiration. Habit is more dependable. Habit will sustain you whether you're inspired or not.
Success is a journey, not a destination. The doing is often more important than the outcome.
Life is not a spectator sport. If you're going to spend your whole life in the grandstand just watching what goes on, in my opinion you're wasting your life.
Give a man a fire and he's warm for a day, but set fire to him and he's warm for the rest of his life.

Albert Schweitzer.bio: Albert Schweitzer was an Alsatian theologian, musician and physician who founded a hospital at Lambaréné in Gabon and served there for decades. His philosophy of reverence for life and his Bach scholarship earned him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1952.

Anais Nin.bio: Anaïs Nin, French-born American diarist and novelist. She is celebrated for her multi-volume Diary, begun when she was eleven, and for works such as Delta of Venus.

Anne Frank.bio: German-born Jewish diarist whose diary documents life in hiding during the Holocaust.

Anton Chekhov.bio: Anton Chekhov was a Russian playwright and master of the short story, a practising doctor who wrote The Cherry Orchard, Uncle Vanya and hundreds of stories. His restrained, humane art reshaped both the theatre and short fiction of the 20th century.

B.R. Ambedkar.bio: Indian jurist and social reformer who chaired the drafting of India's Constitution and campaigned against caste discrimination.

Benjamin Franklin.bio: American polymath - printer, scientist, diplomat - and a Founding Father of the United States.

Bill Watterson.bio: American comic artist (born 1958), creator of the Calvin and Hobbes comic strip.

Charles Dickens.bio: English novelist and social critic; author of A Christmas Carol, Oliver Twist and Great Expectations.

Charlotte Brontë.bio: English novelist, author of Jane Eyre.
Charlotte Brontë.credit: Alonzo Chappel, Public domain (File: File:Charlotte Bronte by Alonzo Chappel.jpg)

Cicero.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman, lawyer and orator considered the master of Latin prose. His speeches, letters and philosophical works, including On Friendship, transmitted Greek philosophy to the Roman world.

Daisaku Ikeda.bio: Daisaku Ikeda was a Japanese Buddhist philosopher, educator and peace activist who led the Soka Gakkai lay Buddhist movement and founded Soka University. He wrote extensively on Buddhism, dialogue and peace.

Desmond Tutu.bio: South African Anglican archbishop and Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1984) who campaigned against apartheid.

Dogen.bio: Founder of the Sōtō school of Zen in Japan and author of the Shōbōgenzō, a landmark of Buddhist philosophy.

Eckhart Tolle.bio: Eckhart Tolle is a German-born spiritual teacher living in Canada, author of The Power of Now (1997) and A New Earth (2005), books on presence and the ego that became international bestsellers.

Elbert Hubbard.bio: Elbert Hubbard was an American writer, publisher and philosopher who founded the Roycroft arts-and-crafts community. His essay "A Message to Garcia" (1899) was one of the most widely reprinted works of its era; he died in the sinking of the Lusitania.

Elie Wiesel.bio: Romanian-born American writer (1928–2016), author of Night.

Emily Dickinson.bio: American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems, mostly unpublished in her lifetime, made her a central figure of American literature.
Emily Dickinson.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress, Public domain

Freddie Mercury.bio: British singer and songwriter (1946–1991), lead vocalist of the band Queen.

Frederick Douglass.bio: American abolitionist and writer who escaped slavery and became a leading voice against it.

Fyodor Dostoevsky.bio: Russian novelist, author of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.

George Bernard Shaw.bio: Irish playwright and critic; author of Pygmalion; Nobel Prize in Literature 1925.
George Bernard Shaw.credit: Sussman, Public domain (File: George Bernard Shaw, playwright (SAYRE 9001).jpg)

Grace Hopper.bio: American computer scientist and U.S. Navy rear admiral (1906–1992), a pioneer of the COBOL programming language.

Henry David Thoreau.bio: American writer known for Walden (1854) and the essay Civil Disobedience.

Jackie Robinson.bio: American baseball player (1919–1972), the first African American to play in Major League Baseball.

Jacques Cousteau.bio: French naval officer and explorer (1910–1997), pioneer of underwater filmmaking and co-inventor of the Aqua-Lung.

Jane Austen.bio: English novelist known for Pride and Prejudice and Emma, celebrated for irony and social observation.
Jane Austen.credit: Engraving by William Home Lizars after James Andrews, Public domain

Jawaharlal Nehru.bio: Leader of India's independence movement and the country's first Prime Minister (1947-1964).

Jiddu Krishnamurti.bio: Indian philosopher and speaker on the nature of mind, meditation, and human freedom; rejected all guru roles.

Jim Henson.bio: American puppeteer (1936–1990), creator of the Muppets.

John Keats.bio: English Romantic poet of the great Odes, including Ode to a Nightingale.

Katherine Mansfield.bio: New Zealand modernist short-story writer, a leading figure of early 20th-century literature alongside Joyce and Woolf.
Katherine Mansfield.credit: Archives New Zealand from New Zealand, CC BY-SA 2.0

Kobe Bryant.bio: American basketball player (1978–2020), 20 seasons with the Los Angeles Lakers and five-time NBA champion.

Leo Tolstoy.bio: Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

Martin Luther King Jr..bio: American Baptist minister who led the civil rights movement; Nobel Peace Prize laureate 1964.

Mary Shelley.bio: English novelist, author of Frankenstein, a founding work of science fiction.

Muhammad Ali.bio: American heavyweight boxing champion and cultural icon known as much for his activism as his titles.

Napoleon Bonaparte.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French in 1804. His Napoleonic Wars reshaped Europe, and his Napoleonic Code influenced legal systems worldwide. He died in exile on Saint Helena.

Ovid.bio: Ovid was a Roman poet celebrated for the Metamorphoses, a vast narrative poem of mythological transformations. Exiled by the emperor Augustus to the Black Sea coast, he spent his last decade writing poems of lament and endurance.

Pearl Buck.bio: Pearl S. Buck was an American writer who spent much of her early life in China, where her parents were missionaries. Her novel The Good Earth won the Pulitzer Prize, and she received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1938.

Pema Chodron.bio: Pema Chodron is an American nun in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition and a widely read author and teacher. Her books, including When Things Fall Apart, bring Buddhist teachings on compassion and difficulty to a broad audience.

Plato.bio: Greek philosopher, student of Socrates and author of The Republic.

Publilius Syrus.bio: Publilius Syrus was a Latin writer of the 1st century BC who was brought to Italy as a slave from Syria and later freed. He is known for his Sententiae, a collection of moral maxims drawn from his mimes.

Robin Williams.bio: American actor and comedian (1951–2014), star of Dead Poets Society and Mrs. Doubtfire.

Simon Sinek.bio: British-American author and speaker (born 1973), known for the book Start With Why and his 2009 TEDx talk on inspirational leadership.

Socrates.bio: Greek philosopher of Athens, central figure of Western philosophy; left no writings.

Sophocles.bio: Sophocles was an Athenian tragedian who wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete. Oedipus Rex and Antigone, his most famous works, set the pattern for Western tragedy.

Steve Irwin.bio: Australian wildlife expert and television presenter (1962–2006), host of The Crocodile Hunter.

Steve Jobs.bio: Co-founder of Apple, Steve Jobs helped launch the personal computer era and later reinvented music, phones and tablets with the iPod, iPhone and iPad. Forced out of Apple in 1985, he founded NeXT and built Pixar into a major studio before returning in 1997 to rescue the company he had started.

Sylvia Earle.bio: American marine biologist and oceanographer (born 1935), known as 'Her Deepness'.

Terry Pratchett.bio: English author (1948–2015), creator of the Discworld series.

Thomas Carlyle.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, philosopher and essayist whose works, including Sartor Resartus and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History, shaped Victorian thought. His history of the French Revolution is regarded as a classic of the genre.

Thomas Jefferson.bio: Thomas Jefferson was an American statesman and Founding Father who wrote the Declaration of Independence and served as the third President of the United States (1801–1809). He founded the University of Virginia and doubled the nation's size with the Louisiana Purchase.

Virginia Woolf.bio: Virginia Woolf was an English writer and a central figure of literary modernism, famous for stream-of-consciousness novels such as Mrs Dalloway (1925) and To the Lighthouse (1927). Her essay A Room of One's Own (1929) became a foundational feminist text on women and writing. With her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own work and that of T. S. Eliot and others.

Voltaire.bio: Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet, was a French Enlightenment writer, philosopher and historian famous for the novella Candide and for his witty defence of civil liberties, including freedom of speech and religion. He was one of the most prolific and influential writers of his age.

Walt Whitman.bio: American poet best known for the collection Leaves of Grass (1855).

Zig Ziglar.bio: Zig Ziglar was an American author and motivational speaker who became one of the most influential sales and personal-development trainers of the twentieth century. His book See You at the Top and his famous line 'Your attitude, not your aptitude, will determine your altitude' reached millions.
